summary: This unit teaches you to receive, store, thaw, prepare, season and cook chicken and other poultry safely: jointing, trussing, spatchcocking, roasting, grilling, frying, stewing and poaching. You will cook Jamaican favourites such as jerk chicken, brown stew chicken, curry chicken and fried chicken, check that poultry is cooked with a probe thermometer, and learn how to hold, cool, store and reheat it without making anyone ill.

blocks.p: Chicken is the most popular meat in Jamaica and on most hotel and villa menus. It is cheap, filling and takes seasoning well, and every cook is expected to be able to joint it, season it and cook it properly. This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees.

Raw poultry is also one of the biggest food safety risks in the kitchen. It often carries **Salmonella** and **Campylobacter**, bacteria that cause serious food poisoning. A cook who undercooks chicken, or lets raw chicken touch salad, can make a whole table of guests ill. So this unit is about **safety and hygiene** as much as about flavour and technique.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and practical tasks in the Centre's training kitchen. In the practical tasks you joint chickens, cook brown stew chicken and jerk chicken, and truss and roast a whole bird. The assessor watches your safety, hygiene, probe checks and clean-up as well as the finished plate.

blocks.note: Temperatures and times in this kit are typical figures. The Centre's recipe cards and food safety plan give the exact ones. Follow them, and ask your instructor if they differ from this kit.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Raw chicken carries bacteria on the skin, in the cavity and in the juices. **Salmonella** and **Campylobacter** are the most common. A very small number can make a person ill. Cooking to the right core temperature kills them. The danger is that they spread from the raw chicken to food that will not be cooked again: salad, bread, cooked meat, fruit, your hands and the board.

Risk
How you prevent it
rows: Raw chicken, its juices and packaging
Use a separate board, knife and tongs for raw chicken
Keep it on the bottom shelf, covered
Wash hands, clean and sanitise surfaces afterwards
Use a sharp boning or cook's knife; board on a damp cloth
Cut away from your body; chop bones on a steady board with a cleaver, fingers clear
Dry the chicken first; lay it into the oil away from you
Never overfill the pan; never leave hot oil alone
Keep a fire blanket near; never use water on burning oil
Use outdoors, away from doors and windows

Burning of the skin and eyes

ul: **Wash your hands** with soap and warm water before you start, after touching raw chicken, and before you touch anything else. Dry them on a clean paper towel.

Use **colour-coded boards**, knives and tongs. A common code is red for raw meat, blue for raw fish, yellow for cooked meat, green for salad and fruit, and brown for root vegetables. Some kitchens use a separate colour for raw poultry. Follow your Centre's code.
Never use the same board, knife or tongs for raw chicken and for cooked chicken or salad without washing and sanitising them first.
Prepare salad and ready-to-eat food **before** raw chicken, or in a separate place, and cover it.
After raw chicken: wash, then sanitise the board, knife, bench and sink area, and wash your hands again.
Use clean cloths and change them often. A wet, dirty cloth spreads germs.
Cover cuts with a blue plaster and a glove, and do not work with vomiting or diarrhoea.
Hold a Food Handler's Permit from the health department, as the law in Jamaica requires for food handlers.

blocks.note: Food safety advice says **do not rinse raw chicken under the tap**. Splashes carry bacteria onto the sink, the bench and nearby food, and rinsing does not make the chicken safe: only cooking does. Many Jamaican cooks wash chicken with lime or vinegar. If your Centre allows it, do it carefully in a clean sink, then clean and sanitise the sink and your hands. Follow your instructor.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Chicken itself is not a common allergen, but coatings, marinades and sauces can contain wheat (gluten), eggs, milk, soya, celery, mustard, sesame or peanuts.
Stuffing often has wheat and sometimes eggs, milk and nuts. Jerk and soy-based marinades can contain wheat and soya.
If the order has an allergy, tell the chef, check the recipe and the labels, use clean equipment and fresh oil, and never guess.
Oil used to fry chicken coated in flour can pick up gluten and traces of other allergens; use fresh oil for an allergy order.
Check the **temperature** with a clean probe. Chilled poultry should arrive at 5 °C or below; frozen poultry at -18 °C or below and frozen hard.
Check the **packaging**: it must be whole, clean and dry, with no leaks. Check the **date** and the supplier's details.
Check the **quality**: see the table.
Reject anything that fails, and report it to your supervisor. Record the temperature.
Put it away quickly, with the chilled or frozen items first.

head: Sign
Fresh chicken
Spoiled chicken: reject
rows: Creamy white to pale yellow skin; pink flesh
Grey, green or dark patches; dull flesh
Hard; no freezer burn; no signs of thawing and refreezing
Soft patches; ice crystals; dry white burn; pools of blood in the pack

head: Item
Storage rule
rows: In the fridge at **5 °C or below**, on the **bottom shelf**, in a covered tray so that the juices cannot drip onto other food. Label with the date.
In the freezer at **-18 °C or below**, labelled and dated. First in, first out.
Covered and labelled, in the fridge, never on the counter.
Cooled fast, covered, labelled and dated, in the fridge **above** raw food.
Kept separate, in the fridge, and used within a day or two.

blocks.note: The fridge order, from top to bottom: ready-to-eat and cooked food at the top, then raw fish, then raw meat, and **raw poultry at the bottom**. Whatever drips will then land on food that is going to be cooked to a high temperature anyway.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Check the fridge and freezer temperatures every day and write them on the temperature log.
Use the oldest stock first (first in, first out).
Do not overfill the fridge; air must circulate.
**Thaw in the fridge**, on the bottom shelf, in a covered tray. Allow plenty of time. As a guide, a whole 1.5 kg bird takes about 24 hours or more, and a box of pieces about 12 to 24 hours.
A whole chicken is thawed when there is **no ice in the cavity** and the **legs move freely**. The flesh should feel soft and the joints loose.
**Never** thaw chicken on the counter, near the stove, in the sun or in warm water. The outside warms into the danger zone while the middle is still frozen.
If you must thaw it quickly, seal it in a watertight bag and put it under cold running water, then cook it straight away.
Cook thawed chicken soon, and **do not refreeze** it unless it has first been cooked.
Pat it dry with kitchen paper before cooking: it browns and fries better.

blocks.note: The danger zone is about 5 °C to 63 °C. Between these temperatures, bacteria multiply fastest. The aim is to keep raw chicken below 5 °C, cook it above 74 °C, and hold it above 63 °C.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Types of poultry and how to prepare them

head: Type
Size and age
Best use
rows: About 1.4 to 2 kg; young and tender
Roasting, grilling, frying, stewing, jerk: nearly everything.
Slow cooking: soup and stock. It is too tough to roast.
Roasting, for special meals; they need longer and care with the core temperature.

ul: **Breast**: white meat, lean and tender, dries out easily. Cooks faster.
**Wing**: small, with little meat and a lot of skin; good for grilling and frying.
**Thigh**: dark meat; juicy and full of flavour; takes longer to cook.
**Drumstick**: dark meat; tougher than the breast; popular with children.
**Back and neck**: little meat; used for stock, soup and stew.
**Giblets**: the heart, liver, gizzard and neck that are often packed inside a whole bird. Take them out before roasting. Use them for stock; the liver cooks very fast and has a strong taste.
**Wishbone**: the V-shaped bone at the neck end of the breast. Taking it out before roasting makes carving easier.

head: Term
What it is
Use
rows: 2 drumsticks, 2 thighs, 2 wings and 2 breast pieces
A bird cut into 4: 2 leg quarters and 2 breast quarters
A boneless breast with the first wing bone left on, skin on
Pan frying and roasting, as a neat portion
A thin, flattened slice of breast
A whole bird split down the backbone and pressed flat
Grilling and roasting: cooks faster and more evenly
A whole bird tied with string so that it keeps its shape
The thigh and drumstick bone taken out

blocks.h: Cutting a whole chicken into 8 pieces

flow: Set a clean board of the right colour on a damp cloth; use a sharp boning or cook's knife
Take out the giblets; pat the bird dry
Lay the chicken on its back; pull a leg away from the body and cut through the skin between the leg and the breast
Bend the leg back until the hip joint pops out; cut through the joint to take off the leg; do the same on the other side
Cut each leg in two at the knee joint, into a thigh and a drumstick
Cut off each wing at the joint, where it meets the breast
Cut along the breastbone and down the rib cage to separate each breast from the back
Cut each breast piece in half across (or keep the breast whole, as the recipe says), to make the pieces the same size
Keep the back and bones for stock; wash and sanitise the board and knife; wash your hands

ul: Cut through the joints, not the bones: it is easier, safer and neater. Feel for the joint with the tip of the knife.
Use a heavy knife or cleaver on a steady board for chopping through bones, and keep your fingers well away.
Cut pieces of equal size so they cook at the same time.

head: Method
How
Why
rows: Take out the giblets and wishbone; season; place the bird on its back; tie the legs together with string and tie the wings close to the body (use a trussing needle if the recipe says).
A neat shape, so it cooks evenly and does not dry out, and carves well.
With strong kitchen scissors or a knife, cut along each side of the backbone and remove it; open the bird out and press down on the breastbone to flatten it.
A flat bird is thinner and cooks faster and more evenly, so the breast does not dry out while the thigh is still raw.

blocks.h: Preparing a supreme and an escalope

ul: **Supreme**: cut the breast from the bone with the first wing bone left attached; clean the bone end; remove the tough tendon; season and cook skin-side down first.
**Escalope**: slice a breast in half horizontally or cut a thin slice across; put it between sheets of cling film and flatten it with a mallet to an even thickness; coat and fry quickly.

blocks.note: Keep bones and carcasses for stock. Never use a carcass that has been left out of the fridge or cooked and left warm for a long time.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Chicken has a mild flavour, so Jamaican cooks build the taste with seasoning. Good seasoning goes into the meat and not only on the skin, so score thick pieces or lift the skin and put seasoning under it.

head: Seasoning
Main ingredients
Used for
rows: Scotch bonnet pepper, pimento (allspice), scallion, thyme, garlic, ginger, black pepper, salt, a little sugar and vinegar or lime juice; often blended
Jerk chicken, cooked slowly over pimento wood or charcoal, or in an oven
Salt, black pepper, garlic, thyme, scallion, onion, a little browning (burnt sugar) and sweet pepper
Jamaican curry powder (rich in turmeric), garlic, onion, thyme, scallion, pimento, salt and pepper
Salt, black pepper, garlic powder, thyme, paprika; flour (and sometimes egg or milk) for the coating
Salt, pepper, garlic, thyme, herbs, oil or butter; lime or lemon

ul: Marinate **covered and labelled, in the fridge**, never on the counter. Many cooks marinate overnight; at least 1 hour improves flavour.
Use a non-metal container (glass, plastic or stainless steel), because acid in the marinade can react with some metals.
Do not marinate for days: acid makes the surface of the meat mushy.
**Do not use marinade that has touched raw chicken as a sauce or to baste cooked chicken**, unless it is boiled for several minutes first. The safest way is to throw it away or to make fresh sauce.
Wear gloves for Scotch bonnet pepper, and do not touch your eyes.

blocks.note: Scotch bonnet peppers are very hot. Wear gloves, keep your hands away from your face, and wash the board and knife afterwards. If a guest or colleague asks for it less hot, remove the seeds and the white membrane, or use the pepper whole in a stew and take it out before serving.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Stuffing inside the bird slows the heat, so the middle of the stuffing may stay below 74 °C when the thigh looks done. Many cooks bake the stuffing in a **separate dish**, so that both the bird and the stuffing cook through.
If you do stuff the bird, fill it loosely just before roasting, never the night before, and check that the stuffing reaches about 74 °C as well.
Cool and store leftover stuffing separately; do not leave it in the cooked bird.

sections.title: Cooking methods and checking that poultry is cooked

head: Method
How it works
Good for
Points to remember
rows: Dry heat in a hot oven, 180 to 200 °C, with a little fat
Pat dry; season; baste; use a probe; rest before carving.
Fierce dry heat from above or below
Turn often; do not char; cook through; keep the grill clean and oiled.
In a pan with a little hot oil
Dry the food; do not crowd the pan; turn once.
Completely covered in hot oil, about 160 to 180 °C (follow the fryer maker's instructions)
Do not overload; dry the chicken or coat it; fry in batches; drain on paper; keep oil clean.
Slow cooking in a covered pot with a little liquid
Brown stew chicken, curry chicken, fricassee
Brown first; simmer gently; add vegetables near the end.
Cooked gently in liquid just below boiling
Chicken breast for sandwiches and salads; soup; boiling fowl
Do not boil hard; use the stock.
Over boiling water, no added fat
Lid on; keep the water boiling.
Even sizes; cover if it browns too fast.

ul: Heat the oil to about 160 to 180 °C. A thermometer, or the fryer's thermostat, tells you the temperature. Oil that is too cool makes the chicken greasy; oil that is too hot browns the outside before the inside is cooked.
Pat the chicken dry. Wet food makes the oil spit.
Lower the pieces **gently, away from your body**, in small batches. Overloading drops the temperature and makes greasy chicken.
Never leave hot oil alone. Keep the fire blanket close.
**If oil catches fire**: turn off the heat if you can safely do so, and cover the pan with a fire blanket or a lid. **Never put water on it**, and never carry the burning pan.
Drain the chicken on kitchen paper and season at once.
Check the core temperature of a piece from each batch.

blocks.h: How to tell when chicken is cooked

blocks.p: Chicken must be cooked **right through**. The reliable way is to measure the core temperature with a **probe thermometer**. Colour alone can mislead: a well-cooked chicken may stay slightly pink near the bone, and a chicken that looks brown may be raw inside.

flow: Clean and sanitise the probe
Push it into the thickest part of the piece (the thigh of a whole bird, or the thickest piece in a batch), not touching bone
Wait until the reading stops moving
It must reach about **74 °C** (or the figure in your Centre's food safety plan)
Write the reading on the temperature log
Clean and sanitise the probe before using it again

ul: **Why avoid bone?** Bone heats up faster than meat and gives a false, high reading.
Other signs: juices run clear, not pink; the flesh is white or brown with no pink near the bone; the leg moves freely. These support the probe reading but do not replace it.
Clean the probe between foods, to stop bacteria passing from raw or part-cooked food to cooked food.
Check that the probe is accurate: in iced water it should read about 0 °C, and in boiling water about 100 °C at sea level.

blocks.note: Some guidance allows lower temperatures held for longer. In the practical, use the figure your Centre gives, which is about 74 °C. Never serve chicken that you are unsure about: cook it more.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: **Rest** a roast chicken for about 10 to 15 minutes, loosely covered, before carving. The juices settle back into the meat, so it stays moist; the temperature carries on rising a little.

Carve with a sharp carving knife on a clean board: remove the legs at the joint, separate the thigh and drumstick, take off the wings, and slice the breast across, or remove each breast whole and slice it.
Carve hot food on a warm plate and serve hot.

head: Dish
Typical time
Note
rows: Roughly 20 minutes per 500 g plus 20 minutes; always probe.
About 40 to 60 minutes on a moderate fire
Turn often; probe the thickest part.
Brown stew or curry chicken (cut up)
Until tender; probe a thick piece.
Slow cooking to soften an old bird.

flow: Cut the chicken into pieces on the bone and trim the extra fat
Season with salt, black pepper, garlic, thyme, scallion, onion and a little browning; cover and refrigerate
Shake off the seasoning and keep it; heat oil in a heavy pot
Brown the chicken well on all sides, a few pieces at a time, so the oil stays hot
Take out the chicken; soften the onion, sweet pepper, tomato and herbs in the pot
Return the chicken with a little water or stock; add a whole unburst Scotch bonnet
Cover and simmer for about 30 to 40 minutes, stirring now and then, until the chicken is tender and the gravy thick
Probe a thick piece for about 74 °C; taste with a clean spoon; adjust the seasoning; remove the pepper and serve hot with rice and peas

ul: **Browning** is a dark liquid made from burnt sugar. It gives colour, not strong flavour. Add a little: too much makes the dish bitter.
Browning the chicken in oil first adds flavour and colour; do not crowd the pot, or the chicken will steam and go grey.

flow: Season the chicken with curry powder, salt, pepper, garlic, thyme, scallion and onion; marinate covered in the fridge
Heat oil in a heavy pot; fry a spoon of curry powder for a minute (do not let it burn): this 'burning' of the curry brings out the flavour
Add the chicken and fry it, stirring, so it takes the colour
Add water, a whole Scotch bonnet and thyme; cover and simmer
Add potato in the last 15 to 20 minutes; it thickens the gravy
Probe; taste; remove the pepper; serve hot with rice
Blend the jerk seasoning; wear gloves for the peppers
Cut the chicken into quarters or pieces; score the thick parts and rub the seasoning in, under the skin as well
Marinate covered and labelled in the fridge, best overnight
Cook slowly over a moderate fire of pimento wood or charcoal, or in an oven, turning often so it browns but does not burn
Probe the thickest part: about 74 °C
Use clean tongs for the cooked chicken, not the raw tongs; rest it, chop it and serve hot with festival, bammy or hard-dough bread

blocks.note: Use a jerk pan or charcoal grill outdoors only, away from doors, windows and anything that can burn. Never use petrol to light it, never leave it alone, and never throw water on the coals. Charcoal gives off carbon monoxide, a deadly gas that you cannot smell. Any marinade left in the bowl is thrown away.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Season the pieces and marinate them in the fridge (many cooks use salt, pepper, garlic and thyme, sometimes with milk or buttermilk).
Coat in seasoned flour. Shake off the extra, so the coating is thin and does not fall off.
Fry in oil at about 160 to 180 °C, in small batches, turning once, until golden and cooked through.
Probe a thick piece from every batch, drain on paper, and serve hot or hold at 63 °C or above.

flow: Take out the giblets and wishbone; pat the chicken dry
Season inside and out, and put herbs or a lime in the cavity (do not pack it tightly)
Truss the bird; rub with oil or butter; place in a roasting tray on a bed of vegetables
Roast at about 180 to 190 °C, basting now and then with the juices
Probe the thickest part of the thigh: about 74 °C
Rest for 10 to 15 minutes; make gravy from the juices; carve and serve

blocks.h: Chicken soup and the boiling fowl

ul: An old hen has tough meat but a lot of flavour. Cook it slowly in water with onion, thyme, scallion and pimento for 2 to 3 hours, skimming the scum, until the meat is tender.
Add pumpkin, yam, coco, carrot, potato and spinners near the end to make a thick Jamaican chicken soup. Use a whole Scotch bonnet and take it out before serving.
Chicken stock from bones and carcasses is simmered gently, never boiled hard. Cool it fast and chill it.

blocks.note: Chicken is part of a Jamaican Sunday meal, with rice and peas, and of a Saturday soup. Guests from abroad often ask for jerk chicken. Be ready to explain how hot it is, and to offer a milder choice.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Serve hot chicken **hot**, on a **warm** plate, with a clean rim.
Weigh or count portions so that each plate is the same and costs are right: for example, a portion of cut-up chicken may be 2 or 3 pieces, or a leg quarter.
Put the chicken in the best place on the plate, keep gravy off the rim, and garnish simply: a sprig of thyme, a slice of lime or tomato.
Serve with the usual accompaniments: rice and peas, festival, bammy, steamed vegetables, salad or coleslaw.

head: Step
Rule
rows: Keep cooked chicken at about **63 °C or above**, in a hot cupboard or bain-marie; check with a clean probe. Hot-holding is not for reheating.

Cool quickly: spread in shallow trays and chill, or use an ice bath or blast chiller. Do not leave it in the pot, and do not put a whole hot pot in the fridge. A common guide is hot to about 21 °C in 2 hours, and then to 5 °C in a further 4 hours.
Cover, label and date; fridge at 5 °C or below, above raw food.
Reheat once only, quickly, to about 74 °C in the centre, checked and recorded. Throw away what is left.
Hot food hot, cold food cold; never top up an old tray with new chicken; throw away what has stood too long.

ul: Do not reheat chicken more than once. Each time it is cooled and warmed, bacteria get another chance.
Leftover cooked chicken that was held warm for hours should be thrown away.
Use cooked chicken for salads, sandwiches or soup only if it was cooled and stored properly.
Use the whole bird: carcass, back and neck for stock; trimmings for soup or sauce.
Trim neatly: do not waste meat on the bones.

Scale recipes by dividing by the number of portions the recipe makes and multiplying by the number you need. For example, if 2 kg of chicken serves 8, then 0.25 kg serves one, and 20 portions need 5 kg.
Record waste so your supervisor can see where money is lost.
Wash and sanitise boards, knives, tongs, trays, probe and surfaces after raw chicken; wash your hands.
Use hot detergent water, then sanitiser for its contact time; air dry.
Let frying oil cool, strain it and store or dispose of it as your Centre says. Never pour it down the sink.
Clean the grill, fryer, oven trays and jerk pan.
Put waste in the right bins and take it out. Record temperatures on the temperature log.

c1.title: Sunday roast at a guesthouse in Black River
c1.text: A guesthouse in Black River is serving roast chicken for 12 guests on Sunday. At 6 p.m. on Saturday, cook Sasha puts four frozen whole chickens on the counter under a cloth to thaw overnight. On Sunday she packs bread stuffing tightly into each bird, ties the legs loosely, and roasts them until the skin is golden. She decides they are done because the skin is brown, and carves them at once as the guests are waiting.

c2.title: Jerk chicken at a beach party in Runaway Bay
c2.text: A resort in Runaway Bay is holding a beach party with jerk chicken for 60 guests. The quarters were rubbed with seasoning at 8 a.m. and left in a covered tub in the shade. The cook turns the pieces with tongs, then uses the same tongs to move the finished pieces to a tray and brushes the leftover marinade over them. A few pieces are black outside, while a thick thigh is still pink at the bone.

c3.title: Fried chicken for a school function in Savanna-la-Mar
c3.text: A school in Savanna-la-Mar is catering a function with fried chicken for 150. Trainee Roxanne puts 3 kg of wet, partly frozen chicken pieces into a deep pot of oil at once. The oil spits and the temperature drops, and the chicken comes out pale and greasy. She notices a small flame on the pot's edge as oil spills over the burner.

c4.title: A busy prep kitchen in Kingston
c4.text: In a hotel prep kitchen in Kingston, trainee Marlon cuts raw chicken on a red board, then slices tomatoes for the salad on the same board with the same knife, and wipes both with a damp cloth. He pulls a cooked pot of chicken stock off the stove and leaves it on the counter for the night. The next day he reheats leftover cooked chicken, takes some out for lunch, puts the rest in the fridge, and reheats it again for dinner.

questions.q: What is the problem with the way Sasha thawed the chickens?
o: Under a cloth, the birds could not get cold enough to thaw
Thawing overnight is too short for four birds to defrost fully
The counter is where raw birds should be kept to stay dry
The outside warms up while the middle is still frozen
questions.why: Thawing on the counter lets the outside reach the danger zone while the middle is still frozen. Thaw in the fridge, in a covered tray on the bottom shelf, and allow plenty of time.

questions.q: How should Sasha have known the birds were fully thawed?
o: The skin feels soft and the bag has turned wet
There is no ice in the cavity and the legs move freely
They have been out of the freezer for about two hours
The wings feel cold and the breast feels firm
questions.why: A whole bird is thawed when there is no ice left in the cavity and the legs move freely. Time or the feel of the skin can be misleading.

questions.q: Why is packing the stuffing tightly into the birds a risk?
o: It makes the skin burn before the chicken has had time to brown
The stuffing absorbs all of the juices, which leaves the breast meat dry
Its middle may stay undercooked even when the thigh looks done
A tightly packed bird will not hold its shape when it is carved
questions.why: A tight stuffing slows the heat, so its middle can stay below 74 °C while the meat looks cooked. Fill loosely, or bake the stuffing separately, and probe both.

questions.q: Sasha judged the chickens done by the colour of the skin. What should she have done?
o: Pierced the skin and looked for blood in the juice
Checked the core temperature of the thigh with a clean probe
Cut a deep slit in the breast to see if the flesh was white
Waited until the skin turned dark golden brown all over
questions.why: Colour can mislead. Push a clean probe into the thickest part of the thigh, away from bone, until it reads about 74 °C, and write it on the temperature log.

questions.q: Why should Sasha not have carved the birds at once?
o: The meat needs to cool to room temperature before it can be cut
The skin would be too soft to cut until it has set again
The juices have not settled, so they run out and the meat is dry
The bones are too hot to separate until they cool down
questions.why: Resting for 10 to 15 minutes lets the juices settle back into the meat. Carved at once, the juices run out onto the board and the meat is drier.

questions.q: What was the safest way to hold the seasoned chicken before it was cooked?
o: In the shade, in a covered tub, as long as it was out of the sun
On ice in an open tray, so that the seasoning can dry on the skin
In a covered, labelled container in the fridge, at 5 °C or below
In a covered container in a cool store room with the vegetables
questions.why: Raw chicken must stay at 5 °C or below. Even in the shade, a hot day keeps the chicken in the danger zone, and bacteria multiply fast.

questions.q: What mistake did the cook make with the tongs and marinade?
o: He turned the chicken too often, which spreads the marinade
He put raw germs on the cooked chicken with the tongs and the marinade
He used metal tongs, which react with the jerk seasoning
He moved the finished pieces onto a tray that was too small
questions.why: Tongs and marinade that touched raw chicken carry bacteria, and putting them on cooked chicken recontaminates it. Use clean tongs for cooked pieces, and throw the used marinade away.

questions.q: Some pieces are black outside, and a thick thigh is pink at the bone. What is the most likely cause?
o: The fire was too fierce, so the outside burned before the inside cooked
The seasoning was too sweet, so it burned before the chicken was cooked
The chicken was too fresh and did not have time to dry out
The pieces were turned too often, so the heat could not reach inside
questions.why: A fierce fire burns the outside before the heat reaches the middle. Cook jerk slowly on a moderate fire, turning often, cut thick pieces to an even size, and probe to about 74 °C.

questions.q: Which preparation would help the thick thighs cook through at the same rate as the breasts?
o: Season them for longer, so the flavour can reach the bone
Spatchcock, or cut even sizes, and score the thick parts
Rub on extra jerk seasoning, which cooks the inside through
Put thick pieces over the hottest part of the fire the whole time
questions.why: Even sizes, a flattened (spatchcocked) bird and scored thick parts help heat reach the middle at the same speed. A hotter fire only burns the outside.

questions.q: Why did Roxanne's chicken come out pale and greasy?
o: Too much cold, wet chicken lowered the oil temperature too far
The oil was too hot, so the coating soaked up grease
The chicken was cooked for too short a time in the oil
The pot was not deep enough, so the oil ran out
questions.why: A big load of cold, wet chicken drops the oil temperature, and food fried in cool oil soaks it up. Dry the pieces, fry small batches and keep the oil at about 160 to 180 °C.

questions.q: Oil has spilled over the burner and caught fire at the edge of the pot. What should Roxanne do?
o: Pour cold water on the flame to cool the oil quickly
Lift the pot outside at once, away from the burner
Beat out the flame with a damp towel, then pour out the oil
Turn off the heat if safe, and smother it with a lid or blanket
questions.why: Water makes a fat fire explode, and carrying a burning pot spreads the fire and burns you. Cut the heat if it is safe, and smother the flames with a fire blanket or lid.

questions.q: Roxanne notices her pieces are different sizes. What is the problem for frying?
o: Large pieces take longer than small ones, so some may be raw inside
Small pieces take longer than large ones, so they dry out
Different sizes cause the oil to spit when they are lowered in
Different sizes make the coating fall off the large pieces
questions.why: Heat takes longer to reach the middle of a big piece. Cut pieces to an equal size, or fry the large pieces first, and probe a thick piece from every batch.

questions.q: A student asks whether to use the same oil for the next day's chicken and for a guest with a wheat allergy. What is the best advice?
o: Use the same oil, because the heat kills any wheat trace in it
Strain the oil through a cloth, and then it is safe to reuse
Use fresh oil in a clean pan, as old oil holds traces of the coating
Use the oil but fry the allergy order first before any other food
questions.why: Oil that has fried flour-coated chicken holds traces of gluten, and heat does not remove an allergen. Use fresh oil and clean equipment for an allergy order, and tell the chef.

questions.q: What should Marlon have done after cutting the raw chicken, before slicing tomatoes?
o: Wiped the board and knife on a damp cloth and carried on
Rinsed the board and knife under cold water, and dried them
Washed and sanitised them, or used a clean green board and knife
Turned the board over and used a different part of the knife
questions.why: Wiping or rinsing does not remove bacteria. Washing with detergent and sanitising, or using separate, colour-coded equipment, stops germs passing from raw chicken to the salad.

questions.q: What is wrong with leaving the pot of stock on the counter overnight?
o: It will lose its flavour as the herbs go cold in the pot
The fat will set on top and cannot be skimmed off in the morning
It will take too long to boil again when it is needed
It stays in the danger zone for hours, and bacteria grow in it
questions.why: A large pot of warm stock stays between 5 °C and 63 °C for hours. Strain it into shallow containers, chill it fast in an ice bath, then cover, label and refrigerate.

questions.q: Marlon reheated the leftover chicken twice. What is the rule?
o: Reheat once only, to about 74 °C, and throw away what is left
Reheat it as often as you like, as long as it is steaming hot
Reheat it twice, provided it was kept covered in the fridge
Reheat it once, but only to a warm 50 °C so it does not dry out
questions.why: Each time food is cooled and warmed, bacteria get another chance to grow. Reheat once only, to about 74 °C in the centre, checked with a probe, and throw away the rest.

questions.q: Where should the raw chicken be stored in the fridge, with the salad and cooked meats?
o: On the top shelf, so it stays coldest and cannot be knocked
On a middle shelf, beside the cooked meats, in a covered tray
On the bottom shelf, in a covered tray, below ready-to-eat food
In the door, because it is the easiest place to reach
questions.why: Raw chicken goes on the bottom shelf in a covered tray, so that its juices cannot drip onto ready-to-eat food below it.

questions.q: A cook wants to use a boiling fowl for a roast dinner. What is the best advice?
o: Roast it in a very hot oven, so that the heat softens the tough meat
Cook it slowly in liquid, as in soup, since the meat is old and tough
Fry it in deep oil, so the outside seals in the juices
Grill it quickly over charcoal, then rest it for an hour
questions.why: An old hen has tough meat and a lot of flavour. Slow, moist cooking softens it. Roasting, frying or grilling would leave it chewy.

questions.q: A trainee says a chicken can be tested for doneness by pushing a probe into the breast bone. Why is this wrong?
o: The bone heats faster than meat and gives a false, high reading
The probe could break against the hard bone and spoil the dish
The breast bone is the coolest part, so it gives a reading that is too low
The probe cannot read through the thick skin over the bone
questions.why: Bone heats faster than flesh and gives a reading that is too high. Push the probe into the thickest part of the meat, such as the thigh, without touching bone.

questions.q: Which cut is a boneless chicken breast with the first wing bone left attached?
o: A supreme
An escalope
A spatchcock
A quarter
questions.why: A supreme is a skin-on breast with the first wing bone left on. An escalope is a thin, flattened slice, a spatchcock is a bird split and pressed flat, and a quarter is a leg or breast with bone.
